draft.title: Metafiction
card: Metafiction is writing that draws attention to the fact that it is a made-up text. It reminds the reader that they are reading a story.
Common methods include a narrator who speaks to the reader about how the story is being told, a character who knows they are in a story, or a text that comments on its own plot or writing.

Here is an invented example. A narrator stops mid-scene to say she could end the chapter now, but readers would complain, so she will let Tom find his keys. The narrator talks about the choice of ending, so the story points to itself.
The effect is to break the illusion that the story is a real window onto events. It can make readers think about how stories are built, why they are told and how much they should trust the teller.
draft.remember: Metafiction makes the reader notice the story as a story.

a.q: Which of these is an example of metafiction?
opts: A narrator admits she is unsure how to end the story
A narrator describes a storm in vivid detail
A character recalls a childhood summer by the sea
A narrator tells the story through one character's eyes
a.why: The narrator talks about the work of writing the ending, so the text draws attention to being a text. The other options tell their stories without commenting on how the story is made, even when they use detail or a close viewpoint.
a.clue: Which narrator talks about the story itself, not what happens in it?

b.q: In Priya's short story, the narrator pauses to admit that a better writer would give this scene a clearer setting, and tells the reader to imagine one. What is the main effect of this on the reader?
opts: It reminds the reader that the story is being constructed
It makes the setting feel more real and detailed
It builds suspense about what happens next
It shows the narrator is a character in the action
b.why: The narrator comments on how the scene is written, so the reader is reminded that this is a made-up text. The comment gives no setting details, so it does not make the scene feel more real. It also says nothing about future events, so it does not build suspense.
b.clue: Look at what the narrator is talking about: the events, or the writing?
